The Stoneyard

raise the arch at the yard's heart — then walk the wall of dry-stone works
self-test …
a heap of wedges
A stoneyard: a walled court where the estate keeps its dry-stone works. In the middle, masons raise an arch — a wall that learned to leave a hole. Nine cut stones, no mortar — and the last one, the keystone, is laid by a hand that never cut the first springer. Until it drops, the ring is only a heap. Drop it, and a single line of pure squeeze threads the stone: the yard's arch locks rigid. Set along the wall, three more works in stone.

safe theorem (Heyman): one line of squeeze that stays inside the stone ⇒ it stands forever. No line ⇒ it falls. The sag & the fall are a faithful render; the EXACT claim is the line of thrust at the joints (self-tested).
a heap — no thrust line yet
Raise the arch — eight stones climb from the springers, but the ring can't stand: it sags into the gap. Drop the keystone and it SNAPS rigid — a line of thrust threads the middle third. Now pull a stone: it's jammed by the squeeze. Lift the keystone back out and the span falls. Tap the three carved stones for what they hold.
